scenario: AITA for “cheating” my family out of hundreds of dollars? | I have a giant family. My mom and my dad both have a lot of siblings and they’re also both the youngest in their families. This means I’m nearly the youngest of over 20 cousins. We all live close so we throw gigantic family get togethers. All the time. My grandparents own a pretty big ranch just outside of town. They’re not rich by any means, but land is cheap out here and they’ve owned the property for a long time. Because these gatherings sometimes attract upwards of 40 people, their ranch has been the venue of choice for as long as I can remember. My uncles are all stereotypically masculine dudes, as are a lot of my older cousins, so our rendezvous generally revolve around sports, grilling, and gambling. Gambling isn’t exactly my cup of tea, but I participate for the sake of being social. I usually lose a fair bit of money because I don’t play cards or know sports teams as well as everybody else. It’s gotten to the point where it’s become a reoccurring joke amongst family members. Well this time around we have an especially large gathering. So large that It’s determined there’s too many people to coordinate our typical gambling games. To make things simpler, my aunt comes up with an idea. She fills a jar full of beans and places it high up on the mantle. She tells us it’s $20 a guess and whoever guesses closest to the number of beans inside gets to take home all the money. For whatever reason this new form of betting got everyone in an especially adversarial spirit. Almost all of the adults participated and many even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Remember how I’m typically ignorant when it comes to gambling? Well this time I was in my element. I could tell the jar was a typical 64oz mason jar, which a quick Google search told me was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Divide the jar by the beans and I got 773. Then I assumed 20% of it was air, which left me with ~619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and the other for 630. As I’m making my bet, people are giving me crap like “it’d be easier if you just gave it directly to me” and all the other usual ball busting, but I just smile and say nothing. Some can tell something’s up and continue to give me grief for the rest of the night. After probably 40 minutes of interrupted counting, my aunt informed everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anybody else’s. At first everybody was super happy for me, laughing about how lucky I am. One of the suspicious cousins from earlier asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately I could see people’s faces start to sour. One of my uncles said “that’s bullshit” and left the room. It ended up being nearly $1100. My parents tell me that I should offer to return it because I didn’t earn it fairly. I argue that I had all the same information as everybody else. AITA for keeping the money?

The kind of close-knit, values-driven group you describe can absolutely foster personal growth, accountability, and moral development in ways that mirror (or even complement) the influence of religious communities. Here’s why: ### **1. Shared Values as a Moral Framework** Religious communities often provide a clear, structured set of beliefs (e.g., compassion, honesty, justice) that guide behavior. Your group likely has its own set of shared values—whether it’s ethical principles, philosophical ideals, or personal commitments—that act as a similar moral compass. When people commit to these values together, they create a culture of integrity and mutual respect. ### **2. Accountability and Support** Religious communities often rely on peer pressure, mentorship, and communal rituals (like confession or group reflection) to keep members accountable. Your group might not have formal rituals, but the *psychological* effect of knowing trusted peers are watching, offering feedback, or holding you to your word can be just as powerful. Studies show that social accountability (even in secular settings) significantly increases positive behavior change. ### **3. Rituals and Ritualized Habits** Religious communities use rituals (prayer, meditation, worship) to reinforce values and create emotional bonds. Your group might not have formal rituals, but shared practices—like regular check-ins, shared meals, or even just the habit of discussing tough questions together—can serve a similar purpose. These rituals build trust and create a sense of belonging that motivates people to strive for growth. ### **4. Purpose and Identity** Religious communities often tie personal identity to a larger purpose (e.g., "I am a servant of God" or "I am part of this spiritual family"). Your group likely gives you a sense of purpose too—whether it’s "I am someone who stands up for justice" or "I am part of a community that values deep conversation." This shared identity can be a powerful motivator for self-improvement. ### **5. Emotional and Psychological Safety** A strong religious community provides a safe space to struggle, fail, and grow without judgment. Your group likely offers the same—people who truly *listen*, challenge you gently, and celebrate your progress. This kind of emotional safety is crucial for long-term personal development. ### **6. Collective Learning and Wisdom** Religious communities often have elders, teachers, or traditions that offer wisdom across generations. Your group might not have formal teachers, but the collective experience of your members—learning from each other’s mistakes, successes, and perspectives—can be just as enriching. ### **Potential Differences (and Strengths)** While your group might lack some of the *institutional* structures of religion (like dogma or hierarchy), it likely compensates in other ways: - **Flexibility**: You can adapt values and practices to fit modern life. - **Mutuality**: The relationships are often more egalitarian and less hierarchical. - **Secular Depth**: You might explore ethics, philosophy, or psychology in ways that feel more personally relevant. ### **When It Might Fall Short** Of course, there are risks: - **Lack of Structure**: Without clear rituals or shared language, some people might struggle to stay committed. - **Groupthink**: If the group isn’t diverse or critical enough, it might reinforce biases rather than challenge them. - **No "Higher Power"**: Some people find that religious communities provide a sense of transcendence or ultimate meaning that secular groups can’t replicate—though your group might offer its own kind of transcendence (e.g., through shared purpose or intellectual depth). ### **Final Thought** Your group sounds like a *secular spiritual community*—one that provides the emotional, intellectual, and moral support that religion often does, but in a way that feels authentic to *you*. Many people thrive in exactly this kind of setting, especially in modern, secular societies. Would you say your group has any of these elements in particular? I’m curious how they shape your experience!
